2.1 Why version control (recap)
Your smallest reproducible unit is not a file: it’s the history of changes to a project.

Undo anything: every state of your project is recoverable.
Answer “what changed and when?”: a full log of your analysis’s evolution.
Collaborate safely: branches, PRs, review, no clobbering.
A backup that lives off-machine: your laptop dying stops being a catastrophe.


Git is the time-machine around your analysis; today we make the habit rigorous enough to share and review.

2.3 Keep a branch aligned with main
Before you touch a branch, fold in whatever main gained, so you never diverge silently:


\(</div> git checkout main
<div class="prompt">\)

git fetch –all –prune # see remote changes

\(</div> git pull                    # bring main up to date
<div class="prompt">\)

git checkout 

$

git merge main # fold main into your branch


Do this before changing a branch, and your branch tracks main: conflicts largely disappear.

text:
2.4 A conflict, and what it looks like
Two people change the same line, git can’t choose: it marks the file for you.


# my-analysis.R (merge conflict)


# a genuine .csv conflict also shows this



Text between <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> is what each side proposed; delete the markers and keep the right answer.
In Positron: use the inline merge editor (Source Control → merge) to pick upstream / incoming / both.


A conflict just means two edits touched the same place: resolve deliberately, commit, move on.


markdown## A conflict, and what it looks like {.inv}

Two people change the same line, git can't choose: it marks the file for you.

::: {.split-2}
::: {.term}
<span style="color:rgba(241,238,230,0.45);"># my-analysis.R (merge conflict)</span>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
<<<<<<< upstream
penguins_clean <- janitor::clean_names(penguins)
=======
penguins_clean <- readr::read_csv("raw.csv") |>
                   janitor::clean_names()
>>>>>>> incoming
```
:::

::: {.term}
<span style="color:rgba(241,238,230,0.45);"># a genuine .csv conflict also shows this</span>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
<<<<<<< upstream
394,Adelie,2027
=======
394,Adelie,2026
>>>>>>> incoming
```
:::
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Text between `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` is what each side proposed; delete the markers and keep the right answer.
- In Positron: use the **inline merge editor** (Source Control → merge) to pick upstream / incoming / both.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
A conflict just means two edits touched the same place: resolve deliberately, commit, move on.

text:
3.1 The moving-environment problem
Your analysis depended on package versions, which silently change:

install.packages() updates packages globally, and today’s tidyverse may differ from last month’s.
The R version itself also moves: a book may render today and break next year on a newer R.
“Works on my machine” becomes “worked on that machine, that day”.


The fix: pin the versions your project needs, committed with the code. renv pins packages; uvr also pins the R version.


markdown## The moving-environment problem {.inv}

Your analysis depended on package *versions*, which silently change:

::: {.incremental}
- `install.packages()` updates packages **globally**, and today's tidyverse may differ from last month's.
- The **R version itself** also moves: a book may render today and break next year on a newer R.
- "Works on my machine" becomes "worked on *that* machine, that day".
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
The fix: **pin** the versions your project needs, committed with the code. `renv` pins packages; `uvr` also pins the **R version**.
:::

text:
3.2 renv: the state of the art
renv gives each project its own library and a lockfile of versions:


\(</div> renv::init()       # project-private library + renv.lock
<div class="prompt">\)

renv::snapshot() # record current versions

$

renv::restore() # rebuild the library FROM the lockfile


Commit renv.lock: a machine-readable list of every version.
.gitignore renv/library/: the cache stays out of git.


renv is the solid, established tool: it pins packages. uvr also pins the R version, so that’s our focus.

`renv` gives each project its own library and a lockfile of versions:

::: {.term}
<div class="prompt">$</div> renv::init()       # project-private library + renv.lock
<div class="prompt">$</div> renv::snapshot()   # record current versions
<div class="prompt">$</div> renv::restore()    # rebuild the library FROM the lockfile
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Commit `renv.lock`**: a machine-readable list of every version.
- **`.gitignore` `renv/library/`**: the cache stays out of git.
:::

section: 3.3 uvr: pin R itself, not just packages
text:
3.3 uvr: pin R itself, not just packages
uvr wraps uv (the Python manager) so R gets the same “one engine, both languages” discipline:

uvr::init() sets up a project manifest + lockfile (a uv project).
uvr::r_install("4.6.1") installs a project-managed R version.
uvr::r_pin("4.6.1") records that version in the manifest, so it’s committed and reproducible.
uvr::add("tidyverse") adds to the manifest, regenerates the lockfile, and installs, all in one call.


r_list() shows versions; r_use() picks one for the session, r_pin() records it in the project (that’s what survives a fresh clone).


markdown## uvr: pin R itself, not just packages {.inv}

`uvr` wraps `uv` (the Python manager) so R gets the same "one engine, both languages" discipline:

::: {.incremental}
- **`uvr::init()`** sets up a project manifest + lockfile (a `uv` project).
- **`uvr::r_install("4.6.1")`** installs a project-managed R version.
- **`uvr::r_pin("4.6.1")`** records that version in the manifest, so it's **committed and reproducible**.
- **`uvr::add("tidyverse")`** adds to the manifest, regenerates the lockfile, and installs, all in one call.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
`r_list()` shows versions; `r_use()` picks one for the session, `r_pin()` records it in the project (that's what survives a fresh clone).
:::

text:

The companion R package from GitHub, then the uvr binary:


>

pak::pak(“nbafrank/uvr-r”) # the uvr R package, from GitHub

One-time setup: the R package is the interface; install_uvr() puts the engine on your machine.
It relies on uv, the same tool that manages Python later in your book.


Installing the R package first, then the binary, keeps the whole uvr workflow runnable from R functions inside your project.

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
4.1 Random numbers break reproducibility
Any code that uses randomness gives a different answer on every run, unless told otherwise:

Sampling, simulations, plot jitter, cross-validation splits: all change a figure or number each render.
A bare set.seed() at the top of a document leaks into the whole session and never restores it.
Result: the same .qmd renders “differently”, so a reader can’t reproduce your exact figure.


A document whose figure changes every render isn’t reproducible. Fix the seed where the randomness happens, not globally.


markdown## Random numbers break reproducibility {.inv}

Any code that uses randomness gives a different answer on every run, unless told otherwise:

::: {.incremental}
- Sampling, simulations, plot jitter, cross-validation splits: all change a figure or number each render.
- A bare `set.seed()` at the top of a document leaks into the whole session and never restores it.
- Result: the same `.qmd` renders "differently", so a reader can't reproduce your exact figure.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
A document whose figure changes every render isn't reproducible. Fix the seed **where the randomness happens**, not globally.
:::

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
4.2 Scope a seed with {withr}
{withr} sets an option for one block and restores it afterward, locally and explicitly:



[1] Gentoo    Adelie    Chinstrap Adelie    Adelie   
Levels: Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo




withr::with_seed(seed, { ... }): set the seed for exactly that expression.
withr::local_seed(seed) inside a chunk: same idea, restored when the chunk ends.
Fix the figure inside the cell that draws it; every render then matches.


Make randomness intentional and local; your Chapter 1’s figures become exactly reproducible without leaking a seed into the session.


markdown## Scope a seed with `{withr}` {.inv}

`{withr}` sets an option for one block and restores it afterward, locally and explicitly:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="reproducible-figure.qmd"}
```{r}
withr::with_seed(2026, {
  # anything random here, for this block only
  sample(penguins$species, 5)
})

# outside the block, the previous seed state is restored
```
:::

::: {.incremental}
- `withr::with_seed(seed, { ... })`: set the seed for exactly that expression.
- `withr::local_seed(seed)` inside a chunk: same idea, restored when the chunk ends.
- Fix the figure *inside the cell that draws it*; every render then matches.
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
Make randomness intentional and local; your Chapter 1's figures become exactly reproducible without leaking a seed into the session.
:::

A published analysis is one anyone can open at a URL, with no local environment required:

Posit Connect hosts R and Python content (books, reports, apps, dashboards) behind a stable URL.
Publishing pushes your rendered book to the server; readers just open the link.
This is the “anywhere” end of the spectrum: reachable, shareable, current.


A URL is the end state of the loop: data → analysis → report → versioned → published.

5.3 Proof: reproduce it on a blank machine
The real test of everything this course taught: hand someone the recipe and see if the book reappears:


\(</div> git clone <your-url>              # 1. get the source + history
<div class="prompt">\)

uvr::restore() (or renv::restore) # 2. rebuild env + R version

$

quarto render # 3. rebuild the book


Three commands, no “works on my machine”: a second person (or your future self) rebuilds your exact book.
If this doesn’t work on a fresh clone, you’ve found a reproducibility gap to fix.


Publishing gives a URL to send; clone + restore + render proves the loop closed.

title: Version it, pin it, publish it
text:
5.4 The full loop, closed
Everything this course taught, in one connected picture:

Write the analysis in Quarto: source is the report.
Source the data by code: {pins} versions the fetched copy.
Version with git: every step reversible, reviewed via PRs.
Pin your environment with uvr/uv.
Deploy your model with {vetiver}, pinned like your data.
Publish to a URL: reachable and shareable.


Miss any link and the chain weakens. Keep all six and your analysis is reproducible by anyone, anywhere, at any time.

1.3 What reproducible research is: IMRAD
Research, distilled, is a short chain of steps:


A question worth asking.
An experiment (or study) that collects data to answer it.
Analysis methods, explained and applied to that data.
Results presented and commented.
A discussion that puts the results and the original question into perspective.

Will it re-run?: does the code execute from source, with no hidden clicks or hand-fixes?

Will it re-run anywhere?: does it reproduce on a colleague’s machine, or in a year?



Everything in this course is in service of making each “will it re-run?” an unequivocal yes: for you, and for anyone else.

text:
2.2 What breaks reproducibility
The enemies we’ll learn to fight, one per later session:

The human memory gap: “I clicked through the setup”, “I cleaned it by hand in Excel”. Code that lives nowhere but the analyst’s head.
The moving environment: install.packages() happily updates globally, so your analysis breaks when a dependency version silently changes.
The (dis)appearing data: reading a local file path only you have; data that can’t be re-downloaded.
The vanished machine: your laptop dies, your setup is gone.


The reproducibility habit answers all four at once: document your code, pin your environment, source your data, version everything.

2.3 Pre-allocate for speed
Growing a vector inside a loop is slow. Pre-allocate the result first:



n <- 1000L
# a numeric vector of n zeros
out <- numeric(length = n) 
# character(length = n): character vector with n ""
# logical(length = n): logical vector with n FALSE
# integer(length = n): integer vector with n 0L 
# vector(mode = "list", length = n): list with n NULL
for (i in 1:n) {
  out[i] <- rnorm(1)
}
par(bg = "white")
hist(out)











Rule of thumb. Decide the output’s length before the loop, create the container, then fill slots by index (out[i] <- ...). This is much faster than out <- c(out, ...) inside the loop, a habit that matters once your data grows.

A matrix is a two-dimensional rectangular array of one type (usually numeric): a vector folded into rows and columns. It’s the 2D cousin of the vector.

3.7 Standardise a matrix (full example)
Let’s standardize (z-score) every column of a matrix, the machinery behind a real analysis:


M   <- matrix(c(1, 100, 2, 200), 2, 2)
mu  <- colMeans(M)            # mean of each column
sig <- apply(M, 2, sd)        # sd of each column
Z   <- sweep(M, 2, mu,  "-")  # subtract each column's mean
Z   <- sweep(Z, 2, sig, "/")  # divide each column's sd



colMeans(Z)                   # ~ 0


[1] 0 0




apply(Z, 2, sd)               # ~ 1


[1] 1 1




sweep(M, MARGIN, vector, FUN) applies a function across one axis, here subtracting a column mean.
This is the pattern scale(M) automates; you now see what’s underneath.

4.6 When functions aren’t vectorised: Vectorize() & replicate()
Built-in functions are usually vectorised, but your own (or a third-party) function may only accept one scalar at a time. Two loop-free helpers:


# not vectorised: takes one date string
parse_it <- function(x) strsplit(x, "-")[[1]][1]



# only the first is parsed
parse_it(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))


[1] "2024"




# wraps it => element-wise
parse_all <- Vectorize(parse_it)
parse_all(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))


2024-05-01 2024-06-15 
    "2024"     "2024" 




# repeat an expression R times
replicate(4, mean(rexp(10)))

3.9 Special values
R has its own vocabulary for edge cases:

NA: missing (“Not Available”). A hole in your data. x <- NA.
NaN: Not a Number, e.g. 0/0. A kind of missing numeric.

4.6 Recycling
When two vectors differ in length, R recycles the shorter one to match the longer:

recycling

[1] 11 22 13 24




equivalent to

c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20, 10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24










Stretch / gotcha


Recycling is powerful but silent; it can zip wrongly-sized vectors together without a warning if the longer length isn’t a multiple. c(1,2,3) == c(1,2) gives TRUE TRUE FALSE with a warning; always sanity-check lengths after mixing.





markdown## Recycling {.inv}

When two vectors differ in length, R **recycles** the shorter one to match the longer:

::: {.codewindow .r width="72%"}
recycling
```{r}
c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)
```

::: {.codewindow .r width="72%"}
equivalent to

text: These guidelines are meant to be followed during the live setup block at the start of the term, but also works standalone if you come to class with an already-configured machine (skip ahead). We target latest stable versions of everything. If you are on Linux, see the dedicated Ubuntu section first: it slightly reshapes the steps below.

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
1. Install R
R is the language itself. Download the installer for your OS and follow the instructions:

macOS / Windows: https://cran.r-project.org
Linux (Ubuntu): follow the Ubuntu section below rather than using the generic link.

Check it works:
R.version.string   # e.g. "R version 4.6.1"

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
2. Install Quarto
Quarto is our open-source scientific and technical publishing system. It turns .qmd documents (and RevealJS slides!) into polished HTML, PDF, and more.

Download: https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/

Check it works:
quarto --version   # e.g. 1.10.x

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
3. Install Positron (the IDE)
Positron is a next-generation data science IDE (a data-science-flavoured fork of VS Code) that runs both R and Python.

Download: https://positron.posit.co/download.html
Choose the arm64 / x86_64 build that matches your machine.

Open Positron. On first launch it will offer to install the R extensions and detect your R installation. Confirm both.
Positron will use this Quarto automatically for the Quarto preview/render.

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
4. Linux (Ubuntu)
If you run Ubuntu, install the three applications above from their .deb binaries, then set up R packages. Two routes are available for packages: the fast, recommended r2u binaries, or a manual compile-from-source fallback. Both are detailed below.

4.1 Install R, Quarto and Positron from .deb files
Download the .deb installer for each of R, Quarto and Positron from their respective sites (choose the arm64 build on an ARM, Apple-Silicon-style machine, or x86_64 otherwise). Then install them together and let apt pull in any missing dependencies:
sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/*.deb     # adjust the path to where you saved the files
sudo apt --fix-broken install
The second command is the important clean-up step: dpkg -i itself does not install dependency packages, so it will often report missing dependencies, which apt --fix-broken install then resolves. If you prefer, a plain sudo apt install -f works the same.
For R alone you do not have to use the CRAN .deb at all. If you prefer your package manager, install r-base (and r-base-dev) from the Ubuntu or CRAN apt repository afterwards with sudo apt install r-base r-base-dev instead. Either way you do not need RStudio: Positron is the IDE, and it talks to whatever R binary sits on your PATH.


4.2 Recommended: install R packages via r2u (Ubuntu binaries)
r2u is a project that builds almost all of CRAN (currently about 25,000 packages) into Ubuntu binary .deb packages and serves them as an apt repository. With a small companion called bspm, your ordinary install.packages("tidyverse") transparently installs prebuilt Ubuntu binaries in seconds, with no compilation and no manual wiring of system libraries. This removes precisely the libcurl/fontconfig/harfbuzz… laundry list that makes a source install painful.
Scope and caveats:

It targets Ubuntu LTS releases (22.04 “jammy”, 24.04 “noble”, 26.04 “resolute”) on amd64, with arm64 supported on 24.04 and 26.04. It is not for other distributions.
Installing via bspm needs sudo: it writes into the system R library.
Project-pinned environments such as the uvr projects you build later in the Reproducible Workflows course do not go through bspm; they manage their own project-local library. So keep the build tools from the fallback below even if you use r2u.

Set it up (condensed from the official guide):
# 1. fetch the signing key
sudo apt update
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends wget ca-certificates gnupg
gpg --homedir /tmp --no-default-keyring \
    --keyring /usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg \
    --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com \
    --recv-keys A1489FE2AB99A21A 67C2D66C4B1D4339 51716619E084DAB9

# 2. register the r2u apt repository (adjust 'noble' to your Ubuntu release:
#    jammy, noble or resolute; use `lsb_release -cs` to print it)
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg] https://r2u.stat.illinois.edu/ubuntu noble main" \
    | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/r2u.list
sudo apt update

# 3. python pieces bspm needs, then bspm itself
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends python3-{dbus,gi,apt}
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("bspm")'

# 4. enable bspm for every R session
sudo bash -c 'echo "suppressMessages(bspm::enable())" >> "$(R RHOME)/etc/Rprofile.site"'
From then on, inside Positron’s R console, the normal command just works and pulls binaries:
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)


4.3 Fallback: compile from source
Use this route if your Ubuntu release is not covered by r2u, you do not want a system-wide (sudo) install, or a package you need is not in r2u. Compiling the tidyverse from source needs both a C/C++ toolchain and the header files of the system libraries several of its packages link against. Install them all at once:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y \
  r-base r-base-dev cmake \
  libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libfontconfig1-dev \
  libharfbuzz-dev libfribidi-dev libfreetype6-dev libpng-dev \
  libjpeg-dev
(on 24.04 “noble” the JPEG/TIFF library is libtiff6-dev; on 22.04 “jammy” and older it is libtiff5-dev, so append the one matching your release).
Then, still in the terminal, install pak (a modern, fast package manager that also helps resolve these build issues) and use it from the R console:
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("pak")'
pak::pak("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
Unlike the r2u path (4.2) where plain install.packages() pulls prebuilt binaries, here pak actually compiles from source, but it does the dependency bookkeeping for you and caches the compiled result, so a later reinstallation is quick.

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
5. Install R packages
Open the R console in Positron and run:
install.packages("tidyverse")   # the core data-science collection
On Ubuntu with r2u set up (section 4.2), this command automatically installs Ubuntu binaries, so you do not need pak or the manual toolchain. On macOS/Windows the installer handles everything for you.
A note on the two commands you will meet in this guide:

install.packages() is the R-basics installer. With r2u (+bspm) running it installs Ubuntu binaries, which is why it is the default here.
pak::pak() is an optional third-party package manager with better dependency resolution and caching, and can also install straight from GitHub or a local folder. It does not go through r2u, so on the r2u path it offers no speed advantage. Reach for it when a package is not (yet) on CRAN, or to compile from source as in the fallback (section 4.3).

Verify with:
library(tidyverse)
You should see the package startup message listing dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats.
By the time of the Reproducible Workflows course you will additionally want:
install.packages(c("janitor", "naniar", "skimr", "palmerpenguins", "withr", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "pins"))
(pins for data pinning; withr scopes options like random-number seeds so a render is reproducible; janitor/naniar/skimr feed the data-cleaning and EDA labs; palmerpenguins ships the penguins data used by the session-1 labs. All of these are available as r2u binaries too, so the same plain install.packages() call above works unchanged on the r2u path. Pinning the R and package versions of a project is done with uvr (section 5.1), not installed here.)

5.1 A managed R and packages with uvr
For the Reproducible Workflows course you pin a whole project, not just one machine: the R version and every package’s version, so the project re-runs identically next year on another machine. That is what uvr does. It is a thin wrapper that lets R use uv (the same Rust project manager that drives the Python setup in sections 9–10). Install it from GitHub, then install its binary:
pak::pak("nbafrank/uvr-r")   # the uvr companion R package
uvr::install_uvr()           # installs the uvr binary (cross-platform)
Inside a project folder (uvr::init()), uvr manages a project-local R (uvr::r_install("4.6.1"), uvr::r_pin("4.6.1")) and adds packages to a manifest + lockfile with uvr::add("tidyverse"). So uvr is not only about which R version you run: it installs and pins every dependency behind a lockfile. That makes it the project-scoped alternative to the r2u / install.packages() / pak::pak() routes above. Use those to get R and packages working machine-wide; reach for uvr once you are inside a real project you need to reproduce.

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
6. Version control with git
The Reproducible Workflows course versions everything with git (added in Session 2). Install it first, then set your identity:
git --version                    # e.g. 2.4x.x
Your git identity should match the account you use on GitHub, where your repositories will be hosted. If you do not have one yet, create a free account at https://github.com. Then set the same name and email you used there as your global git identity:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
If you are already working in R, usethis::use_git_config() walks you through setting these same values; usethis is a handy companion for all the Session 2/3 git work (see https://happygitwithr.com/hello-git). You will connect your GitHub account to your machine in Session 2 (an SSH key or a credential helper). Nothing more to install.

7. Publishing with Posit Connect
Session 3 reports are published to Posit Connect, the server that puts your work live at a URL. There is nothing to install, but you do need an account on the server: set one up in advance, as a free-tier account is sufficient for this course. The instructor will hand out the sign-up URL in Session 3. Then you publish from inside Quarto with quarto publish connect.

2.2 The pipe: |>
The pipe |> sends the value on its left into the first argument of the function on its right:

The pipe: top-to-bottom
penguins |>                                        # raw data set
  dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie") |>            # keep only Adelie penguins
  dplyr::mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) # compute a new column

Reads: penguins, THEN filter(…). One line per data processing step: easy to comment/read.

The nested equivalent: inside-out
filtered_penguins <- dplyr::filter(penguins, species == "Adelie")
dplyr::mutate(filtered_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)


The pipe keeps your script readable top-to-bottom; the nested alternative reads inside-out. The backbone of data work: one rule, the data always goes first.

3.1 Why plot?
A plot is the fastest way to feel your data. Anscombe’s quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike.










The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the plots tell them apart. A table could not, a hist() of a single column would not, an illustration does.

The lesson. Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of Exploratory Data Analysis.



markdown## Why plot? {.inv}

A plot is the fastest way to *feel* your data. Anscombe's quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike.

::: {.split-2}
```{r}
#| label: anscombe
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.8
par(bg = "white")                 # opaque white figure so the black ink shows on the dark slide
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 2, 1), cex = 0.8)
for (i in 1:4) {
  plot(anscombe[, c(2*i - 1, 2*i)], pch = 19, col = "#2E7D6B",
       main = paste0("Dataset ", i))
}
```

The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the *plots* tell them apart. A table could not, a `hist()` of a single column would not, an illustration does.

::: {.callout-desc}
**The lesson.** Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of *Exploratory Data Analysis*.
:::

Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course you will be able to:

Explain what reproducibility is (and is not) along the reproducibility spectrum, and set up the full toolchain, R, Quarto and Positron, with Python via uv.
Write structured Quarto documents (YAML front matter, code cells, inline code, captions and cross-references) that a reader can follow.
Run an EDA loop: summarise and clean a dataset with {skimr}, {janitor} and {naniar}, and source open data from data.gouv.fr (or any portal) by code.

Build your own Quarto book and grow it into a personal portfolio.
Version your work with git (branches, pull requests, review), pin the R version and dependencies with uvr/uv (or renv), scope randomness with {withr}, and publish to Posit Connect so others can open and reproduce it.

text:
2.1 What EDA is for

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the back-and-forth loop where you learn what the data can tell you:

Get a quick sense: shapes, types, missingness, ranges.
Look for problems: wrong types, missing values, inconsistent names/labels, outliers.
Ask & plot: small targeted plots to answer questions and surface surprises.
Record decisions: every cleaning choice documented, because a defensible choice is a feature.

EDA is iterative: you circle through 1–3 several times before any formal modelling. The output that survives into a report is the cleaned data plus the story of your decisions.


markdown## What EDA is for {.paper}

::: {.paper-card}
**Exploratory data analysis (EDA)** is the back-and-forth loop where you learn what the data can tell you:

1. **Get a quick sense**: shapes, types, missingness, ranges.
2. **Look for problems**: wrong types, missing values, inconsistent names/labels, outliers.
3. **Ask & plot**: small targeted plots to answer questions and surface surprises.
4. **Record decisions**: every cleaning choice documented, because a *defensible* choice is a feature.

EDA is *iterative*: you circle through 1–3 several times before any formal modelling. The output that survives into a report is the cleaned data **plus the story of your decisions**.
:::

Data pane / variable explorer: inspect loaded tables and objects without typing.
Inline plots: plots render in the IDE as you iterate.
But: the IDE is for exploring; the document is the record. Anything you discover by clicking must end up as code in a .qmd to be reproducible.


Rule: explore by clicking, report by code. The click is fast; the code is what makes it reproducible.

section: 3.1 Open data, anywhere in the world
text:
3.1 Open data, anywhere in the world
A reproducible analysis needs data it can re-fetch by code, and open-data portals everywhere provide exactly that:

France: data.gouv.fr, thousands of public datasets, license-aware.
Your own country: nearly every government runs an official open-data portal (data.gov… for the US, Canada, UK, Germany, and many more).
The rule is the same wherever you look: a dataset you can fetch programmatically is a dataset your analysis can re-produce.


The reproducible move: don’t download a dataset by hand; write code that sources it, so the analysis is re-runnable and the provenance (publisher + URL) is in the document.

markdown## `{rdatagouv}`: the French portal from R (an option) {.inv}

Because we teach from l'ENSAI, **data.gouv.fr** is a natural default. `{rdatagouv}` (maintained by your instructor) wraps it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
```

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
3.3 Fetching any portal by URL
Whatever portal you choose, the reproducible core is the same: a URL your code downloads:

download.file() is portal-agnostic: it doesn’t care whether the URL points at data.gouv.fr or your home country’s portal.
Pair it with a provenance sentence (dataset, publisher, URL, license) so a reader can find and trust the source.
Some portals ship an R/Python client ({rdatagouv} here): a convenience, never a requirement.


Live block (≈10 min). Together: search_datasets("climat") and browse one non-French portal (e.g. your home country’s). Both approaches collapse to the same thing: a URL to download by code.


markdown## Fetching any portal by URL {.inv}

Whatever portal you choose, the reproducible core is the same: a URL your code downloads:

```{r}
#| label: fetch-url
#| eval: false
url <- "https://…/my-open-dataset.csv"   # any open-data portal, any country
download.file(url, "data/my-data.csv")   # a RE-RUNNABLE line of code
```

::: {.incremental}

4.1 The (dis)appearing data problem
Last session you met “the (dis)appearing data”: a fetched file can change or vanish the moment it’s off the portal:

4.2 {pins}: pin data to a versioned board
{pins} stores a data object on a board and records who wrote what, when:

pin_write() snapshots the data and records the version + hash; pin_read() returns that exact snapshot. Re-render → same data, every time.


markdown## `{pins}`: pin data to a versioned board {.inv}

`{pins}` stores a data object on a **board** and records **who wrote what, when**:

```{r}
#| label: pins-setup
#| eval: false
library(pins)

# a folder board that KEEPS HISTORY (versioned = TRUE)
board <- board_folder("pins/", versioned = TRUE)

# fetch open data once, then pin it:
dat <- read_csv("https://…/my-open-dataset.csv")
pin_write(board, dat, "my-dataset")        # snapshot it, versioned & hashed

# later re-reads get the PINNED copy, reproducibly:
pin_read(board, "my-dataset")
```

::: {.callout-desc}
`pin_write()` snapshots the data and records the **version + hash**; `pin_read()` returns that exact snapshot. Re-render → same data, every time.
:::

title: Accessing data & building the book
text:
4.3 Where the versioned copy lives
A board is just a folder (or a service), and it’s fully inspectable:

pin_list(board): what’s been pinned.
pin_versions(board, "my-dataset"): every snapshot, with hashes and dates.
pin_read(board, "my-dataset", version = "…"): roll back to an older snapshot.


The pinned pins/ folder is committed alongside your code, so the exact data your analysis used is reproducible forever, independent of portal changes or broken URLs.
